new_statements.quote: Con relación al acento de las voces totonacas, se aplican las siguientes reglas: (1) se acentúa la sílaba penúltima de palabras que terminan en vocal breve; (2) se acentúa la última sílaba de palabras que terminan en vocal larga o consonante (con excepción de la explosión glotal); (3) el acento se escribe sobre las palabras que no siguen las reglas anteriores; (4) cuando la u es el segundo miembro del diptongo hallado en la última sílaba de la palabra, el acento cae en el primer miembro del diptongo.
new_statements.translation: Regarding the stress of Totonac words, the following rules apply: (1) the penultimate syllable is stressed in words that end in a short vowel; (2) the final syllable is stressed in words that end in a long vowel or a consonant (except the glottal stop); (3) the accent is written on words that do not follow the preceding rules; (4) when u is the second member of a diphthong found in the final syllable of the word, the stress falls on the first member of the diphthong.

new_statements.relation_note: it was downloaded on 2026-09-16 ( in our check folder) and lies held by the project, so it was re-read and the page re-scanned (spa, 300 dpi) to verify the quote. The catalog record for xico1235 has an empty rule; this supplies the rule: weight-sensitive penult/final with final-heavy attraction (long vowel or consonant, glottal stop excluded) and lexically marked exceptions. Nothing in the catalog contradicts it.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable from the weight of the final syllable: if the word ends in a short vowel (or in a glottal stop, which does not count as a closing consonant), stress is penultimate; if the word ends in a long vowel or a consonant, stress is final. Words that do not follow these rules are marked with a written accent in the dictionary, i.e. there is a lexically marked residue. Rule (4) is an orthographic convention for final -Vu diphthongs (stress on the first vowel).
new_statements.exceptions: Rule (3): words that do not follow rules (1)-(2) exist and are written with an accent mark (lexical exceptions, not enumerated). The glottal stop is explicitly excluded from the consonants that attract final stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Reid et al. 1968, Explanatory Notes p. 19: 'This study is based on the dialect of Totonac spoken in the northern part of the State of Puebla, near Villa Juarez' (Villa Juárez = Xicotepec de Juárez), 10,000-15,000 speakers, data 1952-1965; SIL record subject language 'Xicotepec De Juárez Totonac [too]'. The 1974 dictionary is explicitly of Xicotepec de Juárez, Puebla. Bishop 1979's SIL record also lists [too]. All three works are the same variety as the catalog item.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage (Reid 1991 sec. 1.3, Reglas 1-4) is verbatim in the scanned file we hold and matches the page images of the full-book PDF we hold at pp. 4-7. (2) Deciding source: a 1991 SIL reference grammar by the primary describer of this variety, with an explicit, exception-annotated stress section; it is the most detailed stress description among all works Glottolog (6 refs) and the SIL archive (23 items) list for [too]. (3) downloaded now: Reid & Bishop 1974 dictionary p. 3 states the same rule (penult if final short vowel; final if long vowel or consonant, glottal stop excepted; irregulars marked) -- confirms; Reid et al. 1968 is silent on stress. No non-SIL or instrumental study of Xicotepec Totonac stress was found in the bibliographic records I could open; (4) Coding 'weight'
